Every mechanical watch is a small argument with the twentieth century. Quartz won — decisively, embarrassingly — on every axis that can be measured. A $15 Casio keeps better time in a month than a Patek Philippe does in a week, and nobody argues otherwise, least of all the people spending five figures on the losing side.[\[1\]](#fn1)

So the argument was never about accuracy. It is about what you want time to feel like. A quartz movement ticks the world into equal, discrete jumps; a balance wheel breathes it out at four or eight beats a second, continuous, the seconds hand sweeping like it has somewhere to be. One measures time. The other performs it.

> A mechanical watch does not tell you the time so much as remind you that time is being spent.

The honest case for the mechanical watch is also the unglamorous one: maintenance. A service every five to seven years, a few hundred dollars each time, forever. The watch is not a possession so much as a subscription you hold.[\[2\]](#fn2) And yet that is precisely the appeal — an object that asks something of you, in a drawer full of things that ask nothing.

This is not nostalgia. Nobody mourns the paper map while standing in the rain reading one. The mechanical watch survives because it swapped utility for ritual, and ritual turned out to be the more durable product.

#### Notes

1.  The chronometry trials at Neuchâtel made this official decades ago; the quartz crisis is well documented.
2.  Service intervals vary by manufacturer; five to seven years is the typical published recommendation.
